interactive.title: Inequalities on the number line
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a number line. An inequality's answer is drawn as a shaded stretch of the line with an arrow at its far end, because it carries on for ever. Its end is a circle on the end number: open when that number is left out, as with < and >, and filled when it is included, as with ≤ and ≥. A try-a-number marker can be dragged along the line, and the inequality beside it shows whether that number makes it true. When a move is made to both sides, two points stand for the two sides. Adding or taking away slides both points the same distance, and multiplying or dividing by a positive number stretches both away from zero or squeezes both towards it, so neither overtakes the other. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number mirrors both across zero, drawn as arcs over zero, so the point that was further right lands further left and the sign between them flips. Multiplying by −5 plays in two beats, a mirror across zero and then a stretch, and dividing by −5 a mirror and then a squeeze. One screen solves 7 − 3x ≥ 1 two ways side by side, one route dividing by −3 and flipping, the other adding 3x to both sides first so nothing is divided by a negative, and both end at x ≤ 2. The last puzzle counts loads on an example circuit, so its answer is drawn as the whole numbers 0 to 7 rather than a stretch. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, each drawn as a stretch, and a wrong pick has a number put back in to show where it goes wrong: one it includes coming out false, or one it leaves out coming out true.
interactive.ignores: The puzzles' numbers and the 20 A limit are example values, not figures from any regulation. The line is drawn over a short range, but a stretch carries on for ever, and it holds every number in it, fractions and decimals too, not only the whole numbers marked. Multiplying both sides by zero is never a move here, because it turns both sides into 0.

explain.text:
An inequality has a whole stretch of answers, found with the same undo moves as an equation, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips its sign. An equation such as x + 3 = 7 has one answer, 4, the only number that makes its two sides equal. In an [[inequality]], one side may be greater than or less than the other,[^1] so x > 3, read "x is greater than 3", has many answers. 4 works, 3.5 works, but 3 itself does not. On the number line the answer is a stretch running right from 3 for ever. Its end is drawn as an open circle when the end number is left out, as with > and <, and a filled circle when it is included, as with ≥, "greater than or equal to", and ≤.[^3]

You solve an inequality with the same undo moves as an equation. In 2x + 3 > 11, take 3 from both sides to get 2x > 8, then divide both sides by 2 to get x > 4. Picture the two sides as two points on the number line, with the bigger one further right. Taking 3 from both sides slides both points along by the same distance, so the one that was further right stays further right. Dividing both by 2 halves each one's distance from zero: neither crosses zero, and half of the bigger distance is still the bigger one, so their order stays too. You checked an equation's answer by putting it back in,[^6] and an inequality's answer is checked the same way, with a number from the stretch and one outside it. Try x = 5: 2 × 5 + 3 = 13, and 13 > 11. Try x = 4: that makes 11, which is not more than 11, so 4 gets an open circle.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number is different. Take something true, 10 < 15. Multiplying by −1 mirrors every number across zero, so 10 lands on −10 and 15 on −15. A mirror swaps left and right, so 15, which was further right, is now further left, and −10 > −15. Multiplying by −5 mirrors and stretches, giving −50 and −75, and again −50 > −75. Dividing by −5 mirrors and squeezes, giving −2 and −3, and −2 > −3. So when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the [[inequality sign]] reverses, while a positive number keeps it the same.[^2] In −3x < 12, divide both sides by −3 and flip the sign, giving x > −4. Try x = 0: 0 < 12 is true, and 0 is more than −4. Keeping the sign would give x < −4, but x = −5 then makes 15 < 12, which is false.

A minus sign that just appears does not flip anything. In 3x < −12 you divide by 3, which is positive, so the sign stays and x < −4. In x − 5 > −2 you add 5 to both sides, which slides both together, so x > 3. When you do the same move to both sides, what decides a flip is whether you multiply or divide by a negative number, not whether a minus sign is in sight.[^4] You can even dodge the negative: in 7 − 3x ≥ 1, add 3x to both sides to get 7 ≥ 1 + 3x, then 6 ≥ 3x and 2 ≥ x. Read from the other end, 2 ≥ x says x ≤ 2, the same answer that dividing by −3 and flipping gives. **An inequality's answer is a stretch of the number line, found with the same undo moves as an equation, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the sign.[^2]**

analogy.text: Say two points on a DC circuit read 10 V and 15 V on your meter, black lead on the 0 V rail, so 10 < 15. Swap the leads and every reading changes sign, to −10 V and −15 V. Now the 10 V point reads higher, as −10 > −15. Swapping the leads multiplies every reading by −1, and the order flips just as the sign does.
analogy.breaks: Swapping leads only ever multiplies by −1. Multiplying by −5 also stretches the readings, which swapping leads never does. Moving the black lead to another rail shifts every reading by the same amount, like adding a number, and keeps the order, as dividing by a positive number does too.

practice.text:
- Undo what was done to x, the same way as for an equation, doing each move to both sides.
- Adding or taking away any number, negative or not, keeps the sign.
- Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number keeps the sign.[^2]
- Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses it.[^2]
- If you swap the two sides round, reverse the sign as well, since 2 ≥ x says x ≤ 2.
- Draw the answer: a filled circle for ≤ or ≥, an open one for < or >.[^3]
- Check with a number from the stretch and one outside it.

**Rule of thumb:** A flip comes from multiplying or dividing by a negative number, not from a minus sign being in sight.[^4]

**Worked example:** 4 − 3x < 13. Take 4 from both sides: −3x < 9. Divide both sides by −3 and flip: x > −3. Check: x = 0 makes 4, and 4 < 13 is true. x = −4, outside the stretch, makes 4 + 12 = 16, which is not less than 13.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting to flip, so −5x > 15 gives x > −3. Try x = 0, which that includes: 0 > 15 is false. The answer is x < −3.
- Flipping because a minus sign is there, so 3x < −12 gives x > −4. Try x = 0: 0 < −12 is false. You divided by 3, a positive number, so x < −4.
- Giving one number, as if it were an equation. 2x + 3 > 11 is not x = 4: 4 makes 11, which is not more than 11, and every number above 4 works.
- Using the wrong circle. x ≥ 6 includes 6, so its circle is filled.

checks.label: The two sides in an equation are equal, but in an inequality one side may be greater than (or less than) the other: every inequality here holds for a whole stretch of numbers, while the equation in the explanation holds for just one

You can check the solution by substituting the value into the equation, and an inequality the same way: a right answer's numbers put back come out true inside its stretch and false outside it, and each wrong pick puts back a number that comes out the wrong way, in red

When we divide or multiply an inequality by a positive number the sign stays the same, and by a negative number the sign reverses: on the mirror screen each negative move swaps the two dots and flips the sign, each positive one keeps both, and the positive undo moves keep the order
Every puzzle accepts only the answer that matches its inequality at every number from −20 to 20 in halves (whole loads 0 to 20 on the circuit), and each wrong answer differs from it

Every line of working adds up: at x = 5 the sides make 13 and 11, then 10 and 8, then 5 and 4; at x = −5 they make −15 and −12, then −5 and −4; the moves send 10 and 15 to −10 and −15, −50 and −75, −2 and −3, or 2 and 3; every line of both routes has the same answers as 7 − 3x ≥ 1; and every number put back makes what its row says

The circle is unshaded for < and > and shaded for ≤ and ≥: every stretch is drawn to that rule, its circle on the end number, open or filled (one filled dot for =), running the way the sign points, and the circuit draws only the whole loads in each answer

Only reverse the inequality symbol when you multiply or divide each side by a negative number: on the minus-in-sight screen and the puzzle after it a minus sign is in sight, but every move is by a positive number and the sign stays
Before an answer, a puzzle shows its answers as stretches and puts no number back; a right answer then puts its numbers back on its own line
The marker tries any number: at every half from 0 to 6 it sits on its number, and the line beside it says true exactly when the number is greater than 3

Every demonstration (each move on the mirror screen too) has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends, and a pressed move plays straight away and is done within the same time; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.5 s

applied.problem: Says the meter has nothing to show adding a number, but moving the black lead to another rail shifts every reading by the same amount, which is exactly adding or taking away; "which no meter does" is also broader than the point, which is about swapping leads.

Says every wrong pick is shown with a number it includes coming out false, but several (x = 6 in step 4, x > 5, x < −3) are shown by a number they leave out that works; and multiplying by a positive number above 1 stretches away from zero, not towards it.

"has one answer, because its two sides are equal" gives a false reason: equal sides do not make an answer unique (a formula like R = R₀(1 + αΔT) in i6 has many pairs of values); x + 3 = 7 has one answer because only 4 makes its sides equal.
